# Introduction to Zechariah

    * The priest in filthy clothes ([3:1–10](../03/01.md))
    * The golden lampstand olive trees ([4:1–14](../04/01.md))
    * The flying scroll ([5:1–4](../05/01.md))
    * The woman in a basket ([5:5–11](../05/05.md))
    * Four chariots ([6:1–8](../06/01.md))
3. A crown for the high priest ([6:9–15](../06/09.md))

### Literary Structure

Many interpreters see Zechariah organized using chiasms—mirrored patterns where the beginning and end match, then the second and second-to-last parts match, and so on. Three larger sections show this design: the eight night visions (1:7–6:15), the two fasting messages (7:1–8:23), and the closing oracles (chapters 9–14). Smaller chiasms also appear within individual passages, such as 1:14–17 and 8:9–13.

### What is the Book of Zechariah about?

Zechariah wrote to the people of Judah who returned from being exiled in Babylon. The people of Judah continued to sin, as their ancestors did before they went into exile. Zechariah called the people to repent and to obey Yahweh. And he called them to renew the covenant with Yahweh. Zechariah also prophesied about the Messiah and about Israel finally being victorious over her enemies. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]])

### How should the title of this book be translated?

This book traditionally has been titled “Zechariah” or “The Book of Zechariah.” Translators may decide to call it the “The Book About Zechariah” or “The Sayings of Zechariah.” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

### Who wrote the Book of Zechariah?

The prophet Zechariah wrote this book between 520 and 518 B.C.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### Did Zechariah prophesy before Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai?

Zechariah prophesied before the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He prophesied at the same time as Haggai and continued after Haggai.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### What is the meaning of the term “Israel”?

The name “Israel” is used in many different ways in the Bible. Jacob was a son of Isaac. God changed Jacob’s name to Israel. The descendants of Jacob became a nation also called Israel. Eventually, the nation of Israel split into two kingdoms. The northern kingdom was named Israel. The southern kingdom was named Judah. Zechariah uses the term “Israel” to refer to both the nation of Israel and the northern kingdom of Israel.

### What imagery does Zechariah use in reference to the Messiah?

Zechariah presented the Messiah as both a king and a shepherd. Zechariah said that the Messiah would come and deliver his people. However, the Messiah would also be pierced ([12:10](../12/10.md)) and struck with the sword ([13:7](../13/07.md)). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

### What does the phrase “that day” mean?

Zechariah often spoke of the last days by using the phrase “that day” or “in that day.” When referring to a future “day,” the translator should be aware that the author may be speaking about the last days. If your language wouldn’t use the repetition of “on that day” for stylistic emphasis, find a natural way to do it in your language. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lastday]])

# Zechariah 1 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written in prose with imagery used throughout to portray Zechariah’s vision given by the Lord.

Some translations prefer to set apart quotations. The ULT and many other English translations set lines 1:3–6, 14–17, which are extended quotations, farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text.

### The Eight Night-Visions as a Chiasm

Chapters 1:7–6:8 present eight visions arranged in a mirrored (chiastic) pattern: patrolling horses (1:7–17) match the closing chariot vision (6:1–8); the horns that scattered Judah (1:18–21) match the removal of wickedness in the basket vision (5:5–11); Jerusalem without walls (2:1–5) matches the scroll of judgment (5:1–4); and Joshua reclothed (3:1–10) matches the two anointed leaders, Joshua and Zerubbabel (4:1–14). This chapter contains the first two panels of that pattern.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Visions

This book contains a number of visions given to Zechariah. The images are not ones Zechariah actually saw; rather, they were given to him in a vision or dream. It is important for each of these visions to keep their given meanings and not be interpreted to mean any specific thing.

Zechariah uses two separate dates in this first chapter. When compared to the book of Haggai, Zechariah’s prophecy was proclaimed just a few weeks after the prophecy of Haggai. However, the two men prophesied in two different places: Haggai was in Jerusalem, and Zechariah was somewhere outside of Jerusalem.

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is introduced in prose with imagery used in the rest of the chapter to portray Zechariah’s third vision about measuring lines given by the Lord.

Some translations prefer to set apart quotations. The ULT and many other English translations set the lines of 2:4–13, which are extended quotations, farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text.

# Zechariah 3 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents Zechariah’s fourth night vision: a heavenly courtroom scene in which Joshua the priest stands before the angel of Yahweh while the adversary accuses him (vv.1–5), followed by a prophetic oracle about “the Branch” and the removal of iniquity (vv.6–10).

Filthy garments represent sin and defilement, while clean garments and a clean turban represent purification and restored priestly authority.

# Zechariah 4 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Zechariah 4 is the fifth of eight night visions. The chapter moves from a prophetic vision (a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees) to an explanation, then to an oracle declaring that Zerubbabel will complete the temple “not by might and not by power, but by my Spirit,” and concludes with the identification of the two olive trees as those set apart to serve the Lord of all the earth.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Temple Furniture as Symbol

The lampstand echoes the tabernacle menorah (Exodus 25:31–40). Seven lamps and continuous olive oil flowing through golden pipes symbolized God’s provision for continuous worship and the Spirit’s empowering presence.

### Anointing and Divine Empowering

“Sons of the fresh oil” is an idiom for those set apart for special service. Olive oil consecrated kings and priests; here it represents the Spirit enabling Zerubbabel and his community to complete the rebuilding work.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations

Verses 6–10 contain a series of quotes in which it is difficult to discern who is speaking. The ULT suggests:
* the angel speaks from 6–10
* the angel quotes Yahweh in the middle of verse 6 and beginning of verse 9
* the angel prophetically quotes the people’s reaction at the end of verse 7
* the angel, not Zechariah, is the speaker who received the word of Yahweh in verse 8
* the “me” at the end of verse 9 refers to the angel, this is probably the most contested point, scholars are divided as to if this is Zechariah, the angel speaking to him, or the Angel of Yahweh (read as Jesus)
If there is a translation in your area, you may wish to follow its decisions regarding speakers in this section. If not, you may wish to follow the ULT.

### Mountains as Obstacles

Verse 7 calls a great mountain to become a plain, representing political and practical obstacles dissolving so that Zerubbabel can set the capstone in place.

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents two visions in which an angel interprets what Zechariah sees. The first vision (verses 1–4) shows a flying scroll carrying a divine curse against thieves and false swearers. The second vision (verses 5–11) shows evil personified as a woman sealed inside an ephah and carried away to Shinar.

The angel identifies the woman inside the ephah as “the wickedness,” using a human figure to represent the community’s sin. Translators should preserve this identification without reducing it to a mere symbol.

# Zechariah 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the eight night visions (vv. 1-8) with four chariots dispatched as divine agents, then shifts to a sign-act in which Zechariah crowns Joshua the high priest and delivers the “Branch” oracle (vv. 9-15).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The Branch

The title “Branch” is a messianic designation for a coming king who will build the temple and unite kingship and priesthood on one throne, with “counsel of peace” between the two offices (vv. 12-13).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Nested Quotations

Verses 10-15 contain three levels of quotation as Yahweh instructs Zechariah to speak to Joshua a message from Yahweh of Armies.

# Zechariah 6 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written mainly in prose and tells the last vision of the four chariots in the first part of the chapter.

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetic song in 6:12–13.

# Zechariah 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Zechariah 7 shifts from prophetic visions to prose narrative. A delegation from Bethel asks whether to continue fast in the fifth month, and Yahweh responds with two oracles (vv. 4-7, 8-14) that redirect the question from ritual observance to justice, covenant faithfulness, and mercy.

### Chapters 7–8 as a Mirrored Unit

Chapters 7–8 are shaped as a mirrored (chiastic) unit: the opening question about fasting (7:1–3) is answered at the very end (8:18–19); the first sermon on fasting (7:4–14) is balanced by a second sermon (8:9–17), with the covenant sayings (8:1–8) forming the center.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Fasting as Ritual Mourning

The fifth-month fast commemorated the destruction of Solomon’s temple. Yahweh challenges the people as to whether this practice honored him or merely served the people themselves.

# Zechariah 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophetic oracle (the “burden of the word of Yahweh”) that moves from judgment on the surrounding nations (verses 1-8) to the coming of a righteous, humble king who brings peace (verses 9-10), then to Yahweh’s deliverance and restoration of his people (verses 11-17).

### Chapters 9–14 as a Larger Chiasm

Chapters 9–14 are often read as one long, mirrored (chiastic) structure. This chapter’s judgment on the surrounding nations (9:1–8) is balanced at the very end by Yahweh’s kingship over all the earth (14:16–21), while themes of celebration, the rejection of false shepherds, and mourning for the pierced one recur in matching pairs in between.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The blood of the covenant

In verse 11, “the blood of your covenant” refers to the sacrifices that ratified Yahweh’s agreement with Israel, the basis for his freeing his people.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Verse 1

The first verse has several difficulties. The first set centers on Yahweh’s relationship with Hadrach and Damascus. Many English Bibles translate the preposition here (Yahweh “in” the land) as “against’,” but that preposition does not usually have that meaning. It is also not clear what is resting in Damascus. Is it Yahweh or his word or the burden? What does it mean to be his resting place? For the first set, the text and notes will lean toward an interpretation such as “this prophecy is about some place near Hadrach and Damascus; Yahweh is especially present there right now because he is about to do something.” The second set of difficulties centers on the question of whose eyes are looking at whom? Is Yahweh watching the world and Israelites closely? Are the world and the Israelites watching Yahweh closely (as verse 5 may suggest)? Why (beyond translation)? The text and notes will lean toward the interpretation that Yahweh is watching the world closely. This seems to fit with other parts of the book (4:10, 12:4) and verse 8. If a local translation makes a clear decision, you may wish to follow that. Otherwise you may wish to follow the decisions made here.

### Shifting speakers and personified cities

The speaker shifts between the prophet and Yahweh (first person), and cities such as Tyre and Ekron are personified as women; track these shifts throughout the chapter.

### The Lord

In verse 4 and 14, Yahweh is referred to as “Lord.” While we do not recommend following the custom of translating Yahweh as LORD, if that is the decision your translation has made, you will need to take special care in verse 14 where the text reads “the Lord Yahweh” and follow how you have translated that combination in other places (Ezekiel).

# Zechariah 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This prophetic poem first contrasts Yahweh, who gives rain and guidance, with worthless idols and diviners (verses 1-2), then becomes a first-person divine promise to strengthen and regather his scattered people (verses 3-12).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Shepherds and leaders

The shepherds and male goats represent the people’s leaders, while Yahweh is the true shepherd who cares for his flock.

### Regathering the exiles

Yahweh promises to bring the house of Judah and the house of Joseph (Ephraim, the northern kingdom) back from Egypt, Assyria, and distant lands.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifts in speaker

The chapter alternates between describing Yahweh and Yahweh speaking as “I,” and in verse 11 the referent of “he” is ambiguous. Keep these referents clear.

# Zechariah 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter opens with a poetic taunt of judgment (verses 1-3), moves to a prophetic sign-act in which Zechariah acts as a shepherd (verses 4-14), and closes with a woe oracle against a worthless shepherd (verses 15-17). The ULT sets verses 1-3 and 17 as poetry.

### Shepherds and the flock

Throughout the chapter, the shepherd represents a ruler, and the flock represents the people he leads.

### The two staffs

Zechariah names two shepherd’s staffs “Favor” and “Union;” breaking them signifies the ending of Yahweh’s covenant and of the unity between Judah and Israel.

# Zechariah 12 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a new oracle in which Yahweh promises to defend Jerusalem and Judah against the nations that attack them (verses 1-9), then to pour out grief so that the people mourn over “the one whom they pierced” (verses 10-14). The repeated phrase “on that day” marks these as future events.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The one whom they pierced

In verse 10 the pronouns shift from “me” to “him” for the pierced one. Preserve this ambiguity rather than deciding to whom these pronouns refer.

Zechariah is using the words translated as **The burden of the word of Yahweh concerning Israel** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Here Zechariah is speaking of the message from Yahweh as if it were a **burden**, that is, a heavy load that a person must carry. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The severe word of Yahweh]

Zechariah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here Zechariah is speaking of how Yahweh made the world as if he were **stretching out** a tent to form the heavens and **founding** a building to form the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who made the heavens and who made the earth]

This phrase continues the references to creation. The **spirit** of man represents “life.” The word translated **man** could also be transliterated as “Adam.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the life of a person] or [Adam’s life]
This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

Zechariah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here Yahweh is speaking of **Jerusalem** as if it were a **cup of staggering**, that is, a cup of wine that would make the surrounding nations drunk so that they reel and cannot stand. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a source of helpless reeling for all of the peoples all around]

This could mean: (1) Judah and Jerusalem are besieged. Alternate translation: [And just as Jerusalem is besieged, so is all of Judah.] (2) Judah is going to besiege Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [Judah joins the nations to besiege Jerusalem.]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were a **stone of burden**, that is, a stone so heavy that anyone who tries to lift it injures himself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a burden too heavy for all of the peoples]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **injuring** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [will certainly be severely injured]

The expression **will be injured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will surely injure themselves severely]

Yahweh is using the participle **the ones lifting it** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person, namely, the nations who try to take Jerusalem for themselves. Your language may use participles in the same way. If not, you can translate this participle with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [All of the nations who try to lift it]

The expression **will be gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of the nations of the earth will assemble themselves against it]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **confusion** and **madness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [I will strike every horse so that it becomes bewildered and its rider so that he becomes crazed]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were a **house**, a single household. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Judean people]

Yahweh is using **I will open my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will watch over and protect.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will keep watch protectively]

Note: Yahweh is using **every horse**, **every horse of the peoples**, and **its rider** to represent the whole army of the enemy nations. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **honor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the honored house of David and the honored dweller of Jerusalem]

Here Zechariah is speaking of the descendants of King David, the royal family, as if they were a **house**, a single household. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the royal family descended from David]

Zechariah is not referring to a specific **dweller** of Jerusalem. He means the people who live in Jerusalem in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the residents of Jerusalem]

Note: Zechariah is using **will not be great over Judah** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will not be considered more important than the rest of Judah.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Zechariah is using the adjective **stumbler** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the one who stumbles]

Zechariah says **will be like David, and the house of David, like God** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [will be strong like David was, and the house of David will seem as powerful as God]

Note: Here Yahweh’s direct speech resumes after the narration of the previous verses. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

Here Yahweh is speaking of generously giving his spirit to people as if he would **pour out** a liquid on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will generously bestow]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **favor** and **supplications**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [a spirit that causes me to be pleased with them to plead with me and causes me to be pleased with them]

Quote: וְ⁠הִבִּ֥יטוּ אֵלַ֖⁠י אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־דָּקָ֑רוּ וְ⁠סָפְד֣וּ עָלָ֗י⁠ו

The point of this comparison is that just as people grieve very deeply for **the only one**, that is, an only child who has died, so the people will mourn over the one whom they pierced. The point of this comparison is that just as people grieve bitterly over **the firstborn**, that is, a firstborn son who has died, so the people will grieve bitterly over the one whom they pierced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they will weep powerfully over him, just as people weep powerfully when a firstborn son dies]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the mourning of Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo** was a well-known time of very great grief, so the mourning in Jerusalem will be very great. This could mean: (1) the weeping for King Josiah, who was killed at Megiddo and for whom the people mourned greatly, Alternate translation: [like the mourning for King Josiah at Hadad Rimmon] or (2) the ritual mourning for a god named Hadad Rimmon, or (3) both. You could include this information in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.
The word **Hadad Rimmon** is the name of a place, and the word **Megiddo** is the name of a place.

In some languages, the repeated systematic repetition of the rest of verse 12 through verse 14 may not give a similar emphasis to the deepness and powerfulness of the mourning that will happen. Alternate translation: [the clans of David, Nathan, Levi, and the Shimeite will all mourn very intensely; the men and women will mourn separately, in their own ways]

Zechariah assumes that readers will know that the separation of men and women in public mourning reflects the mourning customs of that society. Translate this so readers do not misinterpret it as marital strife or divorce. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [According to custom, each clan will mourn by itself, and men and women will mourn separately]

Here, **the land** represents the people who live in the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And everyone living in the land will mourn]

Zechariah is repeating the term **clans** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys, that each clan mourns by itself. # Zechariah 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Verses 1–6 are a prose oracle about cleansing from sin and removing false prophets. Verses 7–9 shift to poetry, announcing the striking of Yahweh’s shepherd and the purifying of a surviving remnant.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The Prophetic Cloak

The “cloak of hair” (verse 4) is the rough garment that identified prophets. False prophets abandon this clothing to conceal their identity.

# Zechariah 14 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This closing chapter is a prose oracle about the day of Yahweh: the nations attack Jerusalem (verses 1-8), Yahweh reigns as king (verses 9-11), he strikes the attackers (verses 12-15), and the survivors come to worship him (verses 16-21).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The climax of the book

Zechariah 14:20–21 presents a picture of universal holiness, where ordinary domestic objects carry the same sacredness as the High Priest’s crown. In Exodus 28:36, this inscription belonged exclusively to the High Priest’s golden crown. Here it is stamped on common horse bells and kitchen pots, signifying that in the messianic kingdom, the boundary between the sacred and the everyday is abolished, and all of life and creation becomes completely holy to God. Compare this to Isaiah 11:9 and Habakkuk 2:14, where the holy presence and knowledge of God fill the entire earth.

### The day of Yahweh

The repeated phrase “on that day” marks the time when Yahweh judges the nations and establishes his rule. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/dayofthelord]].

### The Festival of Booths

This was a yearly Israelite festival during which people lived in temporary shelters. Here even the nations celebrate it.
